**Proof.**

Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be bounded and Lebesgue measurable, and suppose
$$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = 0 \quad\text{for all } -\infty < a < b < \infty.$$

Define $F(t)=\int_0^t f(x)\,dx$ (Lebesgue integral, with the convention $\int_0^t = -\int_t^0$ for $t<0$). By hypothesis, for any $a<b$,
$$F(b)-F(a)=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = 0,$$
so $F$ is constant on $\mathbb{R}$. Since $F(0)=0$, we have $F\equiv 0$.

Since $f$ is bounded, say $|f|\le M$, $f$ is integrable on every bounded interval. A standard theorem of Lebesgue integration (the *Lebesgue differentiation theorem*, or more elementarily the *fundamental theorem of calculus for the Lebesgue integral*) states:

> If $g$ is Lebesgue integrable on $[a,b]$, then $G(t)=\int_a^t g$ is differentiable at every Lebesgue point of $g$, and $G'(t)=g(t)$ there. In particular $G'(t)=g(t)$ for almost every $t\in[a,b]$.

Applying this to $f$ on any interval $[-N,N]$: $F(t)=\int_0^t f$ is differentiable a.e. on $[-N,N]$ with $F'(t)=f(t)$ a.e. But $F\equiv 0$ is differentiable everywhere with $F'(t)=0$ for all $t$. Hence
$$f(t)=0 \quad\text{for a.e. } t\in[-N,N].$$

Since this holds for every $N\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\mathbb{R}=\bigcup_{N=1}^\infty [-N,N]$, a countable union of null sets is null, so
$$f=0 \quad\text{a.e. on } \mathbb{R}. \qquad\blacksquare$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
